value.body: Examines physical evidence — for example questioned documents, fingerprints, chemical or biological samples — and writes reports that investigators and courts can use. Government forensic science laboratories employ most forensic scientists; private forensic labs, document-examination and verification firms also hire. The work is lab-based and record-heavy, with strict chain-of-custody rules.

items.label: Typical entry
items.note: Many lab roles expect an M.Sc

items.label: Main employers
items.value: State and central forensic science laboratories; private forensic and verification firms

items.label: Common work areas
items.value: Documents, fingerprints, chemistry / toxicology, biology / DNA, ballistics, digital evidence

value.title: How you get in
value.body: In private labs, freshers start as trainee analysts or lab assistants. Government lab posts (scientific assistant, scientific officer) come through SSC, state PSC or department notices and usually need a science or forensic science degree, often a master's.

value.title: At a glance
items: Government posts are limited and competitive; most need a master's.
Each lab division (documents, DNA, toxicology, etc.) needs specific training.
Reports may need to be defended in court.
